title: From Models to Agents: Building Context-Aware Consumer AI at Scale at DoorDash
gist: DoorDash's head of ML/AI for new verticals details the production stack behind its shift from one-shot recommendation models to agentic commerce: language-native consumer memory blocks, RQ-VAE semantic IDs over 55M SKUs, agentically grounded query-intent resolution, and LLM-distilled relevance labels — with disclosed A/B results including +2.2% conversion from relevance work alone and a +13pp accuracy gain on long-tail intent.

insights.claim: DoorDash is deliberately repositioning from restaurant delivery to a general local-commerce delivery system spanning grocery, convenience, alcohol, retail and flowers, and treats ML/AI at every touchpoint as the prerequisite for that expansion.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: The addressable-market story for DoorDash is no longer restaurant take rate; watch new-vertical GOV mix and whether the AI stack actually converts grocery baskets, which are multi-item and far harder than single-restaurant orders.
insights.quote: A lot of people still think of DoorDash as a restaurant delivery business, but we are actually shaping ourselves up for a time now to be your local commerce delivery system.
insights.locator: A lot of people still think of DoorDash

insights.claim: Grocery shopping is being framed as an inherently multi-step planning and reasoning task, which the speaker argues legacy one-shot prediction personalization structurally cannot serve.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: If multi-step reasoning is the moat in grocery e-commerce, incumbents with only click-based recsys (classic marketplaces) face a re-platforming cost, not an incremental upgrade.
insights.quote: Personalization in the old way, the legacy way of one-shot predictions no longer work.
insights.locator: I'm the head of AI for new verticals

insights.claim: The classical recommendation playbook of clicks, ads and co-purchase association rules is described as still working but no longer where the upside is, with generative AI layered on top of rather than replacing the traditional ML layer.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Signals that genAI spend in commerce is additive infrastructure on top of existing recsys, not a rip-and-replace — implying incremental, not collapsing, demand for classic ML infra.
insights.quote: the classical playbook based on your clicks and ads. We do more of that, like people who buy X also buy Y. Those kinds of things, they work for a while.
insights.locator: Before that, I want to really drive this point home

insights.claim: DoorDash is shifting its consumer representation from dense numerical embeddings to language-native memory snippets because LLM agents cannot interpret embedding vectors.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Agent-readable user state is becoming a distinct data asset class; vendors selling 'agent memory' layers are addressing a real production gap at large consumer platforms.
insights.quote: Agents, if you actually have an LLM, do recommendations for you, they are not going to understand what an embedding means. These are just numbers.
insights.locator: Reading the Consumer - Consumer Memory

insights.claim: DoorDash structures consumer memory across three interacting timescales — long-term memory (dietary preferences, brand affinities), real-time session context (e.g. shopping for a party of 16 instead of a household of 2), and statements made inside an agentic chat that get promoted back into long-term memory.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A reusable blueprint for any consumer-agent product; the three-timescale split is what distinguishes a real memory system from a prompt-stuffing demo.
insights.locator: If you think about memory as like a timescale type thing

insights.claim: Memory systems must support deletion as a first-class operation, since consumer facts such as allergies both appear and disappear over time.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Forgetting is an under-built feature in commercial memory products and a compliance surface (health-adjacent data); a differentiator to check when evaluating memory vendors.
insights.quote: Let's say you did not have an allergy, now you have it, that has to go back into long-term memory. Sometimes we will also recover from allergies, so that needs to be erased.
insights.locator: Let's say you did not have an allergy

insights.claim: Memory blocks at DoorDash are strictly versioned with time-travel capability specifically because A/B testing prompt-optimized memory versions is impossible without version control.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Versioned, experiment-ready memory is the operational bar for production LLM personalization — a concrete requirement to test any 'AI memory' platform against.
insights.quote: Without versioning, we cannot do A/B test.
insights.locator: This is a little bit technical of like how we do this

insights.claim: DoorDash runs GEPA-style prompt optimization to improve the quality of its consumer memory blocks, treating prompts as a tunable, versioned production artifact.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Automated prompt optimization has moved from research curiosity to a shipped component in a top-tier consumer platform's stack.
insights.locator: We do prompt optimization. We run GEPA

insights.claim: Language memory blocks turn out to be a general semantic-matching primitive rather than just agent context, powering substitution logic, cross-item pairing and preference inference in non-agentic ranking models.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: The ROI case for building agent memory does not depend on the agent shipping — it pays back inside the existing recsys, which de-risks the investment.
insights.quote: Memory is a semantic matching primitive. It's not just for the agent's context.
insights.locator: One thing to take away is like, we started this journey

insights.claim: Feeding memory-derived embeddings and a GraphSAGE-style graph model of connected memory blocks into DoorDash's existing recommendation stack produced roughly 10% offline lifts in MRR, with the business-metric A/B test still running.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A quantified proof that LLM-generated user descriptions carry information genuinely complementary to behavioral embeddings — the strongest argument for the whole memory build.
insights.quote: We are already seeing 10% lifts in our MRRs. This is actually currently an A/B test. I cannot tell you how much it led to a lift in real business metrics.
insights.locator: We did that, and we added that to our existing recommendation stack

insights.claim: No single encoding of the consumer wins: DoorDash stacks classical behavioral embeddings, memory-text embeddings and graph embeddings together, and reports compounding improvements each time another encoding is added.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Argues against consolidation onto one representation vendor; ensemble-of-representations means sustained demand for multiple embedding and vector-infra suppliers.
insights.quote: no single encoding wins. You have to do your old school embeddings plus you have to do these memory embeddings plus these graph embeddings.
insights.locator: Extraction and encoding needs to be decoupled

insights.claim: DoorDash decouples memory extraction from memory encoding because the two run on different cadences — extraction tracks how fast a consumer's preferences change, encoding serves downstream applications.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: An architectural pattern to look for when assessing whether a memory product is production-grade or a monolithic black box.
insights.locator: Extraction and encoding needs to be decoupled

insights.claim: DoorDash generates personalized carousel 'blueprints' offline in batch LLM jobs and hydrates them in real time from a Milvus vector database with conventional rankers, explicitly to avoid burning tokens on live LLM calls per consumer per moment.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: The dominant cost-control pattern in consumer genAI: precompute the generative part, serve the retrieval part — which caps inference spend growth even as personalization deepens.
insights.quote: None of that creation of the carousel happens live, and that saves a ton of compute and tokens.
insights.locator: Essentially, there is a Milvus vector database

insights.claim: Batch-generated carousels can still be moment-specific — for example detecting a consumer browsing noise-cancelling headphones and auto-building a price-band-matched Black Friday carousel for them.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Shows generative merchandising reaching retail-event monetization moments, where incremental conversion is worth the most.
insights.quote: It is generative, but it's not live. Not everything in the stack is live.
insights.locator: Like, for example, if we see from your in-session memory

insights.claim: DoorDash uses asymmetric two-tower embeddings — injecting an instruction on the consumer side before embedding — so the model learns retrieval-relevant complements rather than mere consumer-to-consumer similarity, placing consumers and items in one natural-language space.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A cheap, reusable trick that materially changes what a retrieval model learns — the kind of detail that separates teams shipping results from teams shipping demos.
insights.locator: What we're doing there is essentially creating this asymmetric two-tower embeddings

themes.theme: Semantic IDs as the new catalog taxonomy

insights.claim: DoorDash carries 55 million SKUs, and argues random SKU IDs plus coarse backend taxonomies break down for substitution, cold start and any attempt to make an LLM speak the catalog natively.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: 55M SKUs is the scale figure to benchmark DoorDash's retail ambitions against grocery and mass-merchant incumbents.
insights.quote: We have 55 million SKUs, all those SKUs expressed in some high dimensional space, there are neighborhoods in which similar things reside.
insights.locator: There is no relationship. We have 55 million SKUs

insights.claim: Semantic IDs — short tuples of numbers where shared prefixes encode shared meaning — are learned via RQ-VAE iterative residual quantization, functioning like postal codes for items rather than social-security-style random identifiers.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: The clearest available explanation of a technique migrating from media recsys into e-commerce; a diligence question for any retail-AI vendor claiming catalog intelligence.
insights.locator: The way you do it is through this technique called RQ-VAE

insights.claim: Semantic IDs originated at Google, Spotify and YouTube for media recommendation, and DoorDash claims to be among the first to apply them to e-commerce catalogs.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Technique diffusion from ad/media giants into commerce is a repeatable pattern — watch which retail platforms adopt semantic IDs next, as it precedes measurable ranking gains.
insights.quote: This is where semantic IDs come in, which is a very cool idea, came out of Google and Spotify, YouTube.
insights.locator: Reading the Catalog - Semantic IDs

insights.claim: Applied to a single hot-sauce taxonomy node containing thousands of items, semantic-ID clustering surfaced roughly 327 sub-clusters — granularity no human taxonomist would have had time to hand-label.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Quantifies how much catalog structure is invisible to manual taxonomies — the labor-substitution case for automated catalog intelligence.
insights.quote: you will start seeing there reside like 327 subclusters that no taxonomist, no human would have time to go and tag
insights.locator: After we learn it, what happens to this hot sauce cluster

insights.claim: Semantic IDs make retrieval cheaper because the system retrieves a four-number tuple rather than large high-dimensional embeddings, and make cold start cheaper because new catalog items inherit the audience of their existing semantic neighborhood.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A direct serving-cost and time-to-monetization argument for compact discrete item representations versus vector search on every request.
insights.locator: Then retrieval can also be faster because you're not retrieving these humongous embeddings

insights.claim: DoorDash uses semantic-ID neighborhoods plus an LLM that names each cluster to generate 'people also search for' query reformulations, and reports a huge lift from this new approach to related-query generation.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Related-query surfaces are prime ad and discovery inventory; semantically derived suggestions expand the queries a marketplace can monetize beyond observed co-search logs.
insights.quote: Query formulation, we're already seeing a huge amount of lift by doing this new way of understanding our items.
insights.locator: Here's an example. Someone is searching for cream

insights.claim: Query suggestions must be conditioned on the business vertical because the same token carries different meaning across catalogs — 'cream' resolves to heavy cream and full cream in grocery but to cream liqueur and peach liqueur in alcohol.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Vertical-conditioned semantics is a hidden cost of multi-category expansion — one search model per marketplace does not transfer cleanly.
insights.locator: Here's an example. Someone is searching for cream

insights.claim: Sub-category granularity from semantic IDs — knowing a consumer wants only brut champagne rather than champagne generally — is being added directly as a feature to existing rankers with what the speaker calls huge uplifts.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Confirms the pattern that new representations pay off fastest as features in incumbent models, not as standalone replacement systems.
insights.locator: Now that I understand this granular level of what subcategory I like

insights.claim: Because semantic IDs are numeric tokens carrying meaning, small or open-source language models can be trained to emit catalog IDs directly, collapsing the usual two-hop pipeline of LLM suggestion followed by a search lookup.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Generative retrieval that speaks catalog IDs natively could displace the vector-search hop entirely — a structural risk to pure vector-database business models in recsys.
insights.quote: we can now train small language models to directly speak these SIDs
insights.locator: The two other ways that SIDs enable us to do something magical

insights.claim: Semantic IDs are written back into consumer memory blocks, creating a feedback loop where catalog granularity refines the stored user profile that then drives future recommendations.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Compounding data loops between item and user representations are the durable advantage; they get harder for late entrants to replicate over time.
insights.locator: The other thing we can do, going back to our memory blocks

insights.claim: Classical softmax intent classifiers fail for commerce search because winner-takes-all probability collapses genuinely ambiguous queries onto one intent, when multiple intents need to be retained and activated by context such as city and time of day.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Explains why an entire generation of classifier-based search-intent infrastructure is being replaced, and where the replacement budget is going.
insights.quote: The problem with these classical classifiers is that they have this winner-takes-all situation.
insights.locator: Reading the Moment - Consumer Intent

insights.claim: Ungrounded LLMs misclassify real commerce queries in predictable ways — labeling '450 north' a restaurant when it is a hazy IPA craft brew, and 'Better Chew' a pet product when it is a farm belonging in grocery.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that world-knowledge LLMs alone do not solve retail intent; grounding infrastructure, not bigger models, is the buying decision.
insights.quote: Ungrounded LLMs do not work. Classifiers do not work.
insights.locator: Actually, the ungrounded LLM says restaurant

insights.claim: DoorDash resolves query intent by first grounding in its own catalog via semantic retrieval and fuzzy refinement, falling back to agentic web search when the catalog returns nothing, then letting an LLM reason over the union with popularity priors and business rules in a disambiguation layer.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A transferable reference architecture for grounded intent in any catalog business; the catalog-first, web-second ordering is the cost-control decision.
insights.locator: Reading the Moment - Consumer Intent

insights.claim: This grounded intent approach improved intent accuracy on long-tail queries by 13 percentage points, a gain the speaker characterizes as extremely hard to achieve on queries with little engagement signal.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Long-tail query accuracy is where marketplace conversion leaks; a 13pp gain there is the kind of number that funds further AI search spend.
insights.quote: on the long tail queries, we improved accuracy by 13% points
insights.locator: Again, there's a lot of numbers here

insights.claim: DoorDash platformized its agentic grounded search internally so any team needing grounded search can use it, explicitly gaining the ability to choose which search provider to use rather than being locked into Gemini, and saving money as a result.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A named example of a large enterprise building an abstraction layer specifically to avoid grounding-search vendor lock-in — a headwind for providers monetizing grounded-search API calls.
insights.quote: It's also saving us a lot of money because you have the choice of what search to use now. You don't actually have to be beholden to Gemini or something to do these searches.
insights.locator: One kickback we got from this is we built this system

themes.theme: LLM-distilled relevance labels and the economics of re-ranking

insights.claim: Engagement-trained search ranking degrades semantic relevance because users click adjacent items they also wanted, teaching the system that apples are relevant to a banana query.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Names the specific failure mode that caps conversion in click-optimized marketplaces and justifies spending on relevance labels.
insights.quote: If you show them apples, and they had the intent of also buying apples, they will go and click apples. Then the system will learn that, ok, for bananas, apples are relevant.
insights.locator: Refining Relevance - Modernizing Ranking and Retrieval

insights.claim: DoorDash built its relevance training set by starting from 600,000 human-annotated query-item pairs, auditing the error-prone human labels with an expensive large LLM, resolving conflicts with an internal query-to-taxonomy model, then distilling into a cheaper student model to scale past 100 million labeled pairs.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: The canonical teacher-student labeling economics: pay once for a small expensive gold set, then scale 160x with distillation — the reason human annotation vendors face structural pricing pressure.
insights.quote: Humans made a lot of mistakes, actually. Then we used a very expensive big LLM to go and audit that and reevaluate.
insights.locator: What we did was we actually applied LLMs to this problem

insights.claim: The distilled relevance labeler reaches 98% accuracy within one class and 89% exact three-class accuracy at 100 million-plus pairs, a scale and quality the speaker says would have been impossible with humans a few years ago.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Concrete accuracy benchmarks for LLM-as-annotator; useful for pricing the make-versus-buy decision against human labeling vendors.
insights.quote: within one accuracy is 98%. Three-class accuracy is 89%
insights.locator: We could scale up our label pairs to 100 million plus

insights.claim: DoorDash deliberately rejected live LLM re-ranking of search results on cost grounds, instead using LLMs offline to generate labels and training a cheap model to internalize them.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A production verdict against the widely pitched 'LLM re-ranker in the serving path' pattern — a caution for vendors whose value prop depends on per-query LLM calls.
insights.quote: If you did with LLM re-rankers, why don't you just go and say, I'm going to take all search results and re-rank them by LLMs. You're going to run out of money because it's extremely expensive
insights.locator: The takeaway here is that you can do these rankings with engagement only

insights.claim: Adding a tunable relevance head to DoorDash's deep ranking model produced a 1% conversion-rate increase and 0.5% GOV increase in A/B test, with the relevance-versus-engagement tradeoff exposed as a dial operators can crank.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Rare disclosure of AI-attributable marketplace GOV lift; at DoorDash scale a 0.5% GOV move is a directly modelable revenue delta.
insights.quote: conversion rate went up by 1%, which at our scale is huge. GOV went up by 0.5%
insights.locator: We struck this balance by using LLMs to generate the labels offline

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf large embedding models — Qwen3 and multilingual-e5-large — lifted retrieval NDCG only about 5%, while DoorDash's 'Mine and Refine' method using supervised contrastive loss plus circle loss delivered a 17% NDCG gain.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Bigger general-purpose embeddings deliver a fraction of the gain from task-specific loss design — evidence that frontier embedding APIs do not commoditize domain retrieval work.
insights.quote: it went up by 5%-ish by directly using the very large embeddings. Our method, which is using these two kinds of losses to separate out the relevance labels, ended up giving us 17%
insights.locator: Just to put it in perspective that you could do these things

insights.claim: Applying the same 100 million labeled pairs to the retrieval layer added a further 1.2% conversion-rate increase, taking the combined retrieval-plus-ranking relevance gain to 2.2% conversion lift.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that one high-quality label asset amortizes across multiple layers of the stack — the ROI multiple that justifies large one-time labeling spend.
insights.quote: we were able to lift conversion by 2.2% by influencing both the retrieval and the ranking layers
insights.locator: Then, you see that this is another test that we ran

themes.theme: Toward an internal commerce foundation model

insights.claim: DoorDash intends to combine consumer memory, consumer semantic IDs and item semantic IDs into an internal foundation model that predicts a consumer's next action from behavioral sequences, serving homepage, cart complements, search and store pages from one model.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Large consumer platforms building proprietary in-house foundation models over their own behavioral data is a demand signal for training compute that never touches a frontier-lab API.
insights.quote: This is the direction we're going, which is going towards encompassing all these new techniques into a toolbox that lets us build our own internal foundation model.
insights.locator: Bringing it Together - Steerable Recommendations

themes.theme: Agent evaluation and agentic harness engineering

insights.claim: DoorDash's grocery shopping agent prototype, originating from a hackathon, exposes its tools to the agent via MCP and runs session memory and agentic memory alongside each other.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: MCP is showing up as the default tool-exposure layer inside a major consumer platform's agent architecture, reinforcing it as a de facto standard.
insights.quote: It has all the agentic tools exposed to the agent via MCP.
insights.locator: This is the architecture. It has a few things under MCP

insights.claim: Internal employees using the shopping agent typically run 10 to 20 turns per session, adding constraints mid-flow such as a $25 budget cap that force the agent to re-reason over a changed environment.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Real session depth for a commerce agent — a token-cost and latency planning input, and a reality check against single-turn demo benchmarks.
insights.quote: typically it's 10 to 20 turns
insights.locator: These chats can go multi-turn

insights.claim: Agent quality must be evaluated over the whole trajectory rather than per turn, because a shopping mission's success is a property of the full trace including tool calls and environment changes.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Trajectory-level evaluation is the missing product category; per-turn LLM eval tools are insufficient for agentic commerce and leave an obvious gap for vendors.
insights.quote: The quality of these agentic systems is the whole trajectory.
insights.locator: Acting on it All - Building the Infra to Evaluate and Improve Agents

insights.claim: DoorDash scores agent trajectories against a three-dimensional rubric of communication helpfulness, shopping execution success and personalization fidelity, using LLM graders over the full transcript including tool calls.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable rubric for consumer agent quality — the operational answer to 'how do you know the agent is good'.
insights.locator: What we came up with is this multi-dimensional rubric

insights.claim: LLM graders should be given binary good/bad judgments rather than graded scores, because LLMs perform poorly at graded evaluation.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: A hard-won design constraint that invalidates many 1-to-5 LLM scoring pipelines currently shipping in eval tooling.
insights.quote: You cannot do graded stuff with LLMs very well. Good or bad, that's the best way to build these systems.
insights.locator: One thing to take away, for when you're building these systems, binary is the best way

insights.claim: DoorDash puts a coding agent outside the evaluation loop to read raw agent transcripts and autonomously fix tool calls and prompts via GEPA-style optimization — a practice the speaker names 'agentic harness engineering' and reports good outcomes from.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Coding agents used as self-improvement machinery for production agents is an emerging spend category — and a demand driver for coding-agent seats beyond software authoring.
insights.quote: This is the new emergence of what we are calling agentic harness engineering. You use a coding agent as your harness, in some sense, and it goes and fixes everything that's broken in the agent.
insights.locator: What we did at the end was have a coding agent look over all these raw transcripts

insights.claim: DoorDash's agent evaluation stack is three LLMs in a box — a user simulator, a transcript builder and rubric graders — with a coding agent supervising from outside.
insights.speaker: Sudeep Das
insights.so_what: Synthetic user simulation plus automated grading is how agentic products get A/B testable at all; teams without it cannot iterate safely.
insights.quote: we created user simulators, we created transcript builders, and we created rubric graders, the three LLMs that sit inside a box
insights.locator: The main thing to take away is that we created user simulators
